claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native, non-uniform oxide layer.
Annealing Q235 steel in air at approximately 200 °C for 1 hour forms Fe3O4.
The proposed pre-oxidation treatment forms a thin, uniform, and adherent oxide layer.
A coherent Fe3O4 scale enhances the room-temperature aqueous corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
A coherent Fe3O4 scale enhances the molten-salt corrosion resistance of Q235 steel at 700–900 °C.
The pre-formed Fe3O4 layer acts as a physical barrier to oxygen ingress.
The pre-formed Fe3O4 layer acts as a physical barrier to chloride-ion ingress.
Restricting diffusion pathways for oxygen and corrosive species retards oxidation.
Restricting diffusion through the Fe3O4 film limits corrosion-related mass change.
At room temperature, the pre-formed Fe3O4 layer remains stable and protective.
At high temperature, the phase stability and adherence of the oxide determine whether protection persists.
Transformation of the oxide into a porous or non-adherent phase causes corrosion protection to fail.
Pre-oxidized Q235 steel will have lower mass loss than as-received Q235 steel under room-temperature aqueous exposure.
Pre-oxidized Q235 steel will have lower mass loss than as-received Q235 steel during molten-salt exposure at 700–900 °C.
A high-temperature transformation to a porous or non-adherent oxide will produce accelerated corrosion.
Extended exposure times may limit the protective effect of the pre-formed oxide.
The hypothesis may not apply to corrosive media that differ substantially from 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution or 75% Na2SO4–25% NaCl molten salt.
